newsitem.title: BELGIUM: TENNIS-BAD WEEK FOR ANTWERP TOURNAMENT ORGANISERS.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-BAD WEEK FOR ANTWERP TOURNAMENT ORGANISERS.

text.p: The 1997 European Community tennis tournament is exceptional -- but for the wrong reasons, a spokesman for the Association of Tennis Professionals (ATP) said on Wednesday.
"This week is just hell," ATP spokeswoman Ann Christin Waldmann told Reuters.

When top seed Goran Ivanisevic of Croatia pulled out on Tuesday because of tendinitis to his left shoulder, it was the latest in a series of blows to organisers who had been told hours earlier that main crowd puller Boris Becker was out with wrist tendinitis.
Russian Yevgeny Kafelnikov and Australian Open finalist Carlos Moya had already pulled out earlier this month.
To make matters worse, second seed Marcelo Rios of Chile was -- and still is despite a first-round win over Romanian Adrian Voinea -- doubtful with a leg injury.
Sweden's Mikael Tillstrom, who faces Briton Tim Henman on Thursday, has flu and eighth-seeded Dutchman Jan Siemerink, beaten by qualifier Nicolas Kiefer in the first round, had a hamstring injury.

Kiefer himself had stomach trouble in his second-round match against Swiss Marc Rosset on Wednesday and seventh seed and defending champion Michael Stich, who crashed out on Tuesday to fellow German Marc Goellner, has a painful shoulder.
Antwerp organisers find it hard to believe but ATP's medical statistics showed that the overall number of players' injuries and illnesses was steadily going down.
"This is just a really bad week," Waldmann said.

'On-site' withdrawals at tournaments went down from 80 in 1994 and 73 in 1995 to 49 in 1996, she said. The average number of injuries and illnesses per tournament dropped to 2.6 in 1996 from 2.8 in 1990.
Dane Per Bastholt, the ATP trainer in Antwerp, said the organisers were just having bad luck.
"There are periods in the year when players are more vulnerable and I think now is such a period. The other is in the fall (autumn), just after the U.S. Open," Bastholt said.
"It's the change of everything -- surface, weather, continent. Everybody comes back from everywhere," he said.

He said players had now returned to Europe, where the weather is colder, to play indoors after having spent a considerable amount of time in Australia and having played Davis Cup in all parts of the world.

"Here they get small illnesses such as influenza...for me that's a sign that they are tired, there are many who talk about their programme being too full. But its that time of the year when everybody is (vulnerable) but players...are even more vulnerable than other people," he said.
Waldmann said the ATP has adopted a number of measures to improve medical treatment for the players.
It now has four full-time trainers who are linked through E-mail to streamline treatment of players.
"Becker for instance, whatever the diagnosis, it will be communicated to the (ATP trainer) in the next tournament so he will be treated in the same way there," Waldmann said.
Doctors at tournament venues now have better medical equipment, Waldmann said. In addition, the ATP has set up a medical committee which meets regularly and its doctors hold a conference each year.
Waldmann noted players could not pull out of a tournament unless the ATP trainer signed their medical certificate.
"Only the trainer can sign the certificate...it is not in our interest to see guys like Becker and Ivanisevic pull out."
